<timestamp>Wednesday, Jun 17, 2026, 7:57 PM (UTC+8)</timestamp>
<user_query>
I have fundamentals on how back propagation work but I am not really prepared to do research in the AI fields yet. (I just graduated from univeristy), how am I able to learn about AI and progress in this field?
</user_query>

Great question, and a healthy place to be — knowing the basics of backprop is genuinely the hardest conceptual leap, and everything after that is mostly a matter of depth and breadth.

Here's a concrete path I'd suggest, roughly in order. You can do these in parallel, but the order helps you not get lost.

## 1. Lock in the math foundation (1–2 months)

You have backprop intuition, which means you've already touched the key ideas. Make the rest of the math rigorous:

- **Linear algebra**: eigenvalues, SVD, matrix calculus — Strang's MIT OCW lectures or *Mathematics for Machine Learning* (Deisenroth).
- **Probability & statistics**: distributions, Bayes, MLE/MAP, information theory. Bishop Ch. 1–2 is enough.
- **Calculus & optimization**: convexity, gradient methods, SGD variants, convergence. Boyd's *Convex Optimization* is overkill but Ch. 1–5 is gold.

You don't need to master all of this — you need fluency so papers don't scare you.

## 2. Learn ML end-to-end before going deep (2–3 months)

- Take one solid course and **do all the assignments in code**:
  - Andrew Ng's ML specialisation (breadth, practical)
  - Fast.ai (bottom-up, you build real models fast)
  - Or *Dive into Deep Learning* (d2l.ai) — free, code-first, PyTorch or TF.
- Implement from scratch (on small data): linear/logistic regression, a decision tree, k-NN, SVM, then a small NN.
- Learn **PyTorch** properly — tensors, autograd, `nn.Module`, dataloaders, training loops. This is your daily tool.

At the end you should be able to take a dataset, pick a model, train it, debug why it's not working, and report numbers.

## 3. Start reading papers (ongoing, starts here)

This is the single biggest differentiator between "knows ML" and "can do research."

- Start with **surveys and "awesome lists"** to map a subfield.
- Then read the **seminal papers** of that subfield in chronological order (e.g. for LLMs: transformer → GPT-1/2/3 → InstructGPT → RLHF papers → Llama papers).
- For each paper, follow this loop:
  1. Skim intro/figures/conclusion first.
  2. Read carefully, writing a 1-page summary: *problem, why prior work fails, their key idea, how they'd evaluate, what I'd do next.*
  3. Try to **implement the core idea** on a toy problem. Even a broken reimplementation teaches you more than 10 papers read passively.

Good habits: keep a paper-reading log, use [paperswithcode.com](https://paperswithcode.com) to find code, and join a reading group (lab, Discord, or Twitter/X ML community).

## 4. Pick a subfield and go deep (3–6 months)

Trying to learn "all of AI" is a trap. After 2–3 you'll naturally gravitate. Common entry points with relatively low hardware barriers:

- **NLP / LLMs** — easiest to start (small open models + Kaggle/free Colab GPUs work for fine-tuning).
- **Time series / spatiotemporal** — given your trajectory simplification work, this is a natural bridge. There's active research on trajectory foundation models, streaming simplification, and graph-based methods.
- **Reinforcement learning** — conceptually elegant, harder to do empirically without compute.
- **Vision / multimodal** — well-trodden, good mentors and benchmarks.

Pick one and learn it like you're writing a mini-thesis on it.

## 5. Do real research (the actual transition)

Reading papers makes you literate; research makes you a researcher.

- **Find a mentor / lab.** Email professors with: a specific paragraph about why their work excites you, what you've built/read, and a concrete 1-page research proposal. Attach your GitHub. Cold emails work surprisingly often.
- **Reproduce a paper** as a first project. This is the most common on-ramp and a strong signal to a lab.
- **Publish something**, even a workshop paper or a strong blog post with code. AIME, NeurIPS workshops, ICML Workshops, or arXiv preprints are all valid.
- **Open source contributions** (Hugging Face, PyTorch, vLLM, etc.) are respected and visible.

## 6. Useful context on "AI research" as a career

A few honest notes that aren't usually said upfront:

- Modern AI research is **very compute-heavy** at the frontier. As a beginner you can absolutely do meaningful work on efficiency, data, theory, evals, or small-model fine-tuning without a GPU cluster.
- The most transferable skill is the **research taste loop**: notice a gap → read what's around it → propose a small experiment → run it → write it up. Practice this on your own projects, not just in a lab.
- Twitter/X, arXiv-sanity, and [thegradient.pub](https://thegradient.pub) are good ambient exposure. Hacker News for the broader scene.

## Concrete 12-month plan if you want one

| Month | Focus |
|---|---|
| 1–2 | Math refresh + d2l.ai or Fast.ai |
| 3 | PyTorch fluency, implement a paper-toy |
| 4–5 | Deep dive into one subfield, read 20+ papers |
| 6 | Reproduce a paper end-to-end |
| 7–8 | Start a small original project; email 10 professors |
| 9–10 | First research artifact (report / preprint / PR) |
| 11–12 | Apply to PhD, research engineer roles, or research labs |

Your existing trajectory-simplification work actually counts as a research-flavored project — algorithms, experiments, comparisons, writing it up. Lean into that as a portfolio piece.

If you want, tell me which subfield pulls you most (LLMs, RL, time series, vision, theory) and I can suggest a more specific reading list and a small starter project to reproduce.
